The Temptation to Keep Adding Features One of the hardest parts of building a product isn’t coming up with new ideas. It’s deciding which ideas not to build. When you’re working on your own app, it’s surprisingly easy to convince yourself that another feature will make it better. Maybe users need more options. Maybe a new screen would make the experience feel more complete. Maybe adding something competitors already have will make the product more attractive. I’ve had these thoughts while building my own apps. And the problem is that most of these ideas sound reasonable. You can almost always find a good argument for adding another feature. But there’s an important difference between something that could be useful and something users actually need . If every product decision comes from our own assumptions, we eventually risk building an app that does a little bit of everything without being particularly good at anything. This is how feature creep can begin. Not necessarily with one terrible decision, but with a series of small, seemingly reasonable additions. The app becomes more complicated, the experience becomes harder to navigate, and the original reason people wanted to use it starts getting lost. I’ve started thinking about feature prioritization differently because of this. Before asking what else I could add to an app, I try to understand what I can make easier. Every Product Starts With a Promise When we first design a product, we usually have a fairly clear idea of the problem we’re trying to solve. That idea shapes the product strategy, the user experience, and the decisions we make about what belongs in the app. For example, a productivity app might promise to help people organize every part of their lives. Another might focus on helping people complete just a few important things each day. Both are valid approaches, but they lead to very different products. The second app doesn’t necessarily need projects, folders, complex calendars, or dozens of productivity tools. Adding those features might make it more powerful, but it could also make it less focused. This is something I try to keep in mind when working on my own products. A new feature shouldn’t change the reason someone chose your app in the first place. Of course, products evolve. User needs change, and sometimes the original idea needs to be reconsidered. But I think there’s a difference between evolving a product because you’ve learned something meaningful about your users and expanding it simply because you have another idea. That distinction became much clearer to me while building Tody. What Building Tody Taught Me About Feature Prioritization Tody is a small productivity app I built around a simple idea: choose three tasks for the day and focus on completing them. No overwhelming to-do lists. No complicated planning system. Just three tasks and a clear place to start. The three-task limit was intentional. I wanted to reduce the number of decisions people had to make before actually doing something. And that constraint became an important part of the product’s identity. But after people started using the app, I noticed something interesting. Some users were entering the same tasks again on different days. Things like exercising, reading, or studying weren’t necessarily one-time activities. They were tasks people wanted to repeat regularly. At first, this didn’t seem like a reason to build a completely new feature. The problem was relatively small: users had to type something they had already entered before. So I introduced autocomplete. When someone started typing a task they had previously added, Tody could suggest the existing text. It was a small UX improvement, but it addressed a specific point of friction. Users didn’t have to write the entire task again. And importantly, nothing about the core experience changed. They still chose up to three tasks. They still focused on one task at a time. I hadn’t expanded what Tody was supposed to do. I had simply made an existing action easier. When a Small Improvement Wasn’t Enough As I continued observing how people used Tody, I noticed that certain tasks kept appearing. Autocomplete helped with typing, but users were still going through the same process of entering those tasks again. That made me reconsider the problem. Maybe the real user need wasn’t just faster typing. Maybe people needed a simple way to reuse tasks that were already part of their routines. That’s when I decided to introduce Saved Tasks.
